decision.reason: All 120 pw paths bit-exact on judge; none beat r6; m=128 5-8x slower than cuBLAS. Cause: per-row bulk copies of x per stage + per-chunk producer/consumer handshake. Restructure as x-stationary CTAs (pw2).

hypothesis.claim: A packed-weight streaming tensor-core GEMM ('pw') beats r6 on the four BF16 layers at m in {16, 32, 128}, and holds or beats it at m in {1, 8}. Weights use r6's judge-proven lossless 12-bit codec in A-fragment order (swap-AB: W rows are the mma M dimension, tokens the n8 dimension), so each layer moves 1.5 B/weight instead of 2. prepare() re-lays the 1536 B units per BN-row block as [n-block][chunk][tile][1536], so any K-slice of an n-block is one contiguous range. That range is streamed once, either through a per-warp register ring of ld.global.nc.L1::no_allocate.v4 (D=3-4 chunks deep) or through 6-12 KB cp.async.bulk stages into a 4-6 deep smem ring with full/empty mbarriers. x is staged in the same ring by 1D bulk copies per token row, with a 16 B row pad so the B-fragment loads are conflict-free. K is split across CTAs to fill 132 SMs, and the partial sums meet through red.global.add.v4.f32 in a fragment-ordered fp32 workspace. The last-arriving CTA converts to bf16, writes out, and re-zeroes its slice and counter, so there is no memset, no second kernel, and graph replays stay consistent. At m=128 the 12-bit stream is about 12 us for pooler at 4.2 TB/s, and mma.sync at roughly 1.6 clk per m16n8k16 per SM is about 13-14 us. That puts pooler/unpooler m=128 near 15-17 us against r6's 20.3/19.3.
hypothesis.compile_check: nvcc 12.8 -arch=sm_90a -cubin -O3 -Xptxas -v on KERNELS_SRC (13 instantiations): compiles in about 3 s, 13/13 with 0 bytes stack frame and 0 bytes spill. Registers are listed in design.register_budget. The full CUDA_SRC (kernels + glue) also compiles with -std=c++20 against a minimal torch mock, because the local CPU torch wheel lacks the CUDA c10 headers. The real torch glue has not been compiled locally.

design.codec: r6 _pack + _c12(dv=1) unchanged (exactness proven in prepare by _unc12; a failed proof makes every pw path decline). Escapes (values whose exponent falls outside the 16-binade window: zeros, tiny or huge values) are fixed in registers by XOR from per-consumer-warp lists. The lists are CSR, one sentinel-terminated list per warp, built per launch geometry and loaded on demand (warp-uniform __ldg). Real weights give at most 4-20 entries per warp.
design.k_wrap_hook: The producer reads x columns (chunk*64) % K and the launcher only requires KCW*64 to be a multiple of K. A router mode with W' = [hi | lo] along K (KCW = 2K/64) needs only an fp32 output variant of pw_put, not a restructure.
design.operands: mma.sync.m16n8k16.row.col bf16 -> f32. A = decoded W unit (16 rows x 16 k per step, r6 order {row g, row g+8, row g k+8, row g+8 k+8}), B = x (16 k x 8 tokens). K is permuted within each 64-chunk exactly as r6's _pack: lane t owns k = 16t..16t+15, step q uses 16t+4q..+3, and B registers are the lane's 16 contiguous bf16 of the token row.
design.reduction: Split-K over gridDim.y with an uneven split (stage ranges ks*NST/KS), KS chosen per path as about 1 or 2 waves of the measured CTAs/SM (_pw_ks). Partials: red.global.add.v4.f32 per fragment into ws[nb][tile][tokentile][lane][4], only for lanes holding a valid token. Then __threadfence, __syncthreads, and an atomicAdd on cnt[nb]. The last arriver does __threadfence, then __ldcg reads, a bf16 store to out, a __stcg zero, and cnt[nb]=0. KS==1 stores straight from registers. Each path and shape has its own workspace and counters, so a broken variant cannot poison another's validation.
design.register_budget: acc RT*TTW*4 + decoded A RT*16 + B 8 transient + ring D*RT*12 (+12 current). ptxas -v, CUDA 12.8 sm_90a, every instance 0 bytes spill: r64t1 96, r32t1 93, r64t2 100, r64t4 121, b64t1 48, b32t1 48, b64t2 51, b64t4 70, b32t4 71, b128m 160, b64m2 160, b64m1 98, r64m 210. ptxas rounds a 5-warp CTA up when capping registers (MINB=2 at 160 threads capped at 168 and spilled), so r64m and b64m1 use MINB=1.
design.stream_variants: MODE 0 ring (register ring, D=4 for m<=32, D=3 at m=128) and MODE 1 bulk (cp.async.bulk 1D, CPS=2 chunks per stage = 12 KB at BN=64, 6 KB at BN=32; CPS=1 at m=128 = 12 KB at BN=128). Smem ring ST=4 (6 for BN=32, 3 for r64m). Empty barrier count = consumer warps, full barrier = 1 arrive.expect_tx(m*CPS*128 + W bytes).
design.tiles: CTA = BN W rows x all m tokens x one K-slice. BN = WN*RT*16 is 32 or 64 for m <= 32, and 64 or 128 for m = 128. At m=128 the x re-read from L2 is (N/BN)*m*K*2 B: 2.7x the packed W bytes at BN=64 and 1.3x at BN=128, so BN=128 is the main m=128 variant.
design.verification_done_offline: A CPU emulator (scratchpad emu_pw.py) mirrors the kernel's address formulas, byte decode (prmt), escape-list walk, PTX m16n8k16 fragment maps, fragment-order workspace and last-arriver scatter. It ran on 7 geometries (ring/bulk, BN 32/64/128, m 1/8/16/32/128, uneven KS, injected zeros/tiny/huge weights): random rows match fp64, one-hot rows are bit-exact. Mutations (dropped escape lists, wrong unit layout) are caught.
design.warp_ownership: Consumer warp (wn, wt) owns RT 16-row tiles x TTW n8 token tiles. Ring mode has WTOK=1, so each W unit is loaded by exactly one warp. Bulk mode at m=128 uses WTOK=2 (64 tokens per warp) with RT=2, so each x B-fragment is reused 2x and each W unit 8x per warp. smem traffic is about 176 B per mma. One extra producer warp per CTA issues every bulk copy.

hypothesis.kill_if: Kill the pw family if every BAKE line shows each pw variant INVALID or ERROR. Also kill it if the best valid pw variant is slower than the r6 'yours' figure minus the ~1 us judge offset on all of pooler m=128, pooler m=32 and qkv m=32, with pooler m=128 above 19 us. Refine instead of kill when one stream type (ring or bulk) or one m bucket wins and the others lose. If prepare hangs or the CUDA context dies (a kernel fault or deadlock the bake-off cannot catch), reject pw1 as an execution failure. That is not evidence against the mechanism; fix the kernel and re-check.

paths.not_served: router (all m), m=256, every odd m -> torch fallback. A -w2 entry declines when its KS equals the -w1 KS.
paths.pw-b128m-w1: bulk BN=128, 8 consumer warps (RT=2 x 64 tokens), 1 CTA/SM, m=128
paths.pw-b64m1-w1: bulk BN=64, 8 consumer warps (RT=1 x 64 tokens), m=128
paths.pw-b64m2-w1: bulk BN=64, 4 consumer warps (RT=2 x 64 tokens), 2 CTAs/SM, m=128
paths.pw-r64m-w1: ring BN=64, 4 warps x 128 tokens, 1 CTA/SM, m=128
paths.pw-r64t1-w1, pw-r64t1-w2: ring BN=64, m in {1, 8}, all four BF16 layers (unpooler n=1024)

risks: A hang (mbarrier deadlock) or an illegal address cannot be caught by the bake-off: it kills prepare or the CUDA context and the check fails outright. Mitigations: the barrier and parity scheme is the r7 producer/consumer pipeline that ran on this judge; the launcher range-checks every size (m, N, BN, KCW, KS, workspace, counter and offset lengths) and returns an error, which becomes a Python exception and a BAKE ERROR line, instead of launching; x is bulk-copied only when contiguous and 16 B aligned (otherwise that call uses the fallback).

m=128 may be limited by the fp32 vector reductions (m*N*KS floats: 8.4 MB for pooler at KS=4) or by the last arriver's serial 32-64 KB read, rather than by mma or HBM. The bake-off keeps r6/cuBLAS on any shape where pw loses.

m=128 smem bandwidth (about 176 B/mma for b128m/b64m2, 256 B/mma for r64m) and mma.sync issue rate may cap it near 15-18 us. 128 small (128 B) bulk copies per stage at m=128 may throttle the producer/TMA.
The small-m ring variants have short per-CTA streams (KCS 2-21 chunks), so ramp-up and the reduction tail may dominate unpooler m<=8 (6.3 MB). The w1/w2 KS pairs let the bake-off choose.

Prepare time: 22 paths. m=1 validation is K one-hot launches per path and layer (8 paths x 21.5k calls at about 100 us each, roughly 20 s), plus the c12 packs (4 layers, 3 BN layouts, about 0.6 GB) and compile. The harness's 240 s guard skips the remaining variants if the budget runs out.

Requires PTX ISA 8.x (red.global.add.v4.f32, cp.async.bulk, mbarrier expect_tx), i.e. CUDA >= 12.1. An older judge toolkit fails the compile, prepare logs 'PREP compile failed', and everything runs on the fallback.
target_shapes: unpooler m=1 <= 3.5 (r6 4.88)

decision.reason: check 7715c850ff89450a: 9/9, 4386.8 us; m=128 paths still lose to cuBLAS (pooler best wk2 31.7 vs torch 28.9 in-prepare). PROBE ladder pooler m=128 64x2: L1 W+x 25.4, L1 no-x 20.9, +decode 24.6, +wgmma 30.1, full 34.6 vs bare bulk stream 17.2 -> four separate costs: cluster-2 skeleton 3.7, x tiles 4.5, wgmma not hidden 5.5, epilogue 4.5. Ring depth 8 and k-split each gain 2-3 us only. Parked pending m<=32 results; analysis-only follow-up.

hypothesis.claim: pw9's wgmma path lost to cuBLAS at m=128/256, but the SASS shows only about 125 hot instructions per stage per warp (3 LDS, 16 PRMT, 4 HGMMA), so the decode is not the limit. The bake numbers give about 570 cycles of fixed latency per stage plus the MMA time: pooler m=128 is about 830 clk per stage and m=256 about 1090; the difference is the extra MMA time. Deferring each slot's release until wgmma.wait_group (required, because wgmma reads x asynchronously) leaves about 2 of the 4 ring stages in flight. Hypothesis: the pipeline is latency-bound, not throughput-bound. pw10 measures that directly with a PROBE ladder, and tests it alongside three alternatives in one check: ring depth 8 (5 at m=256), a wait_group(0)-per-stage control, BN 128 with clusters <= 2 (half the x L2 traffic), and a 2-warpgroup intra-CTA k-split (twice the decode width).
hypothesis.kernel_count: 33: 15 pwc (m<=32 and router m<=32, SASS identical to pw9), 10 wgmma path kernels, 4 wgmma probe kernels, 4 small pw6 probe kernels (kept in the source but no longer called). pw9's router wgmma (wr) and pw8's rg128 / pw-rtg128 are dropped. Local -cubin about 9 s (pw9 6 s); judge compile was 36 s for pw9.
hypothesis.kill_if: If the PROBE ladder shows L1 (stream + handshake only, no decode, no wgmma) already within 3 µs of L4 (full path), the latency is in the TMA/mbarrier skeleton itself (as for m<=32), and the wgmma family stops. If L1 is near the 17 µs stream but L3 (+wgmma) jumps, the MMA/stage interaction is the cost, and the depth-8 and k-split lines show which fix works. Kill the family if no variant beats torch on pooler and unpooler m=128.
hypothesis.kspl_design: KSW = 2: the warpgroups kg = 0, 1 share BN = 64 rows; warp = kg*4 + tile. Each loads its 16 B low-byte block (a + 512 kg) and the stage's code words (kg ? z,w : x,y), decodes its two k16 steps into A[0..7] and issues two wgmma with descriptor offset 4 kg (+2). Branch-free on purpose: a first version branched on kg around the wgmma, and ptxas reported C7520 ('wgmma serialized due to compiler-inserted WG.AR in divergent path'). Escapes: each warp's list holds all entries of its tile (_pw_esc with WTOK = 2), applied with register offset 8 kg (pw_fix3), so entries of the other warpgroup's steps match nothing. Epilogue: warpgroup 0 stages its D in fragment order, warpgroup 1 adds its D after a consumer barrier, then the pw9 cluster epilogue. Empty barriers count all 8 consumer warps; each warpgroup's own wait_group covers its own wgmmas before it releases.

lines.L1 no-x: As L1 with x tiles skipped (expect_tx = W bytes only). L1 minus this isolates the x re-read cost (128 MB from L2 for pooler at BN 64). Prediction: 17-18.
lines.L1 wait+release: Producer streams x tiles (TMA) and W chunks (bulk) exactly as the path does; consumers only wait on the full barrier and release the slot immediately. Prediction: about 18-20, near the bulk-stream probe (17.2) plus the x L2 traffic.
lines.L2 +decode: L1 plus the 3 LDS + decode + escape walk per stage. Prediction: L1 + about 1 (decode is about 125 issue slots per stage per warp).
lines.L3 +wgmma: L2 plus the wgmma batches with the deferred release (no epilogue). If release-after-wait_group starves the ring, this is where the time jumps. Prediction: about 29 (pw9's full time minus the epilogue).
lines.L4 full: The w1d4 path with the cluster epilogue. Expected about 34 (pw9 w1n128a 34.4); L4 - L3 is the epilogue.

probe_plan.where: prepare(), after STATS and before the bake-off, <= 10 s. Pooler m=128 on the w1d4 kernel (= pw9 w1n128: BN 64, one consumer warpgroup, ring 4, KS 2 = 64 x 2 = 128 CTAs; probes launch without clusters because they skip the epilogue). 'PROBE ladder <name> <grid> <us>', timed like the bake-off.

hypothesis.register_budget_ptxas: nvcc 12.8 sm_90a, all 0 spill, 0 stack (a first version indexed A with a runtime k-group offset and had 128-144 B stack frames; fixed): w1d4 138, w1d8 138, w1d8z 106, w2c2 168 (setmaxnreg), wk2 168 (setmaxnreg), v1d4 203, v1d5 202, v1d5z 173, v2c2 168 (setmaxnreg), vk2 168 (setmaxnreg); probes pL1 28, pL1x 22, pL2 43, pL3 138. No LDL/STL in any wgmma kernel, no ptxas C7519/C7520 messages. Pipelining in SASS: w1d8 and wk2 run ARRIVE -> HGMMA batch -> DEPBAR.LE gsb0 0x1 -> release; w1d8z runs DEPBAR 0x0 per stage.
risks: Ring depth 8 at m=128 uses 177 KB of smem and the BN 128 m=256 variant 221 KB: 1 CTA/SM. Pooler w2c2 gives only 64 CTAs (kept for the x-traffic signal, as instructed).
If the PROBE ladder places the cost in L1 (the TMA/mbarrier skeleton), no kernel-side change here can fix it; that is the same finding as for m<=32.
The k-split doubles the consumer warps (384 threads); each warpgroup's partial is summed through smem at the end (about 32 KB at m=128, 64 KB at m=256).

sass_per_stage_per_warp.brief_estimate: The brief's ~1100 instructions per stage per warp was about 10x high: one warp decodes one 16 x 64 unit (1024 weights) per stage, not 16.
sass_per_stage_per_warp.method: cuobjdump: instructions between consecutive WARPGROUP.ARRIVE inside the main loop; 'hot' excludes the escape-hit body (16 SEL, its ISETPs, the list LDG)
sass_per_stage_per_warp.pw10 wk2: 114 / 96: 2 LDS, 8 PRMT, 2 HGMMA per warp (the stage's decode spread over 8 warps)

target_shapes: pooler m=128: in-prepare <= 25 vs torch 30.2 (pw9 best 34.4)
m=256: pooler <= 30 (torch 34.0), unpooler / qkv / o below torch

variants.ks_rule: mode a (w1d4 / v1d4, = pw9): the largest KS in {1, 2, 4, 8} with NB*KS <= 132; mode c2 (all others): the largest KS in {1, 2} with NB*KS <= 132. No cluster of 4 or 8 is generated.
variants.m128: pw-w1d4 (pw9 w1n128, ring 4, mode a; within-run reference), pw-w1d8 (ring 8, 177 KB, 1 CTA/SM), pw-w1d8z (ring 8, wait_group(0) + release every stage: no MMA/decode overlap, every slot freed as early as possible), pw-w2c2 (BN 128, 2 consumer warpgroups on separate rows, ring 6, KS <= 2: pooler 32 x 2 = 64 CTAs, o / unpooler 64 x 2, qkv 18 x 2), pw-wk2 (BN 64, 2 consumer warpgroups on the same 64 rows splitting every stage by k16 steps {0,1} / {2,3}, ring 8, KS <= 2). Five per (layer, m).
variants.m256: pw-v1d4 (pw9 w1n256), pw-v1d5 (ring 5, 191 KB), pw-v1d5z (ring 5, wait_group(0) per stage), pw-v2c2 (BN 128, ring 5, 221 KB), pw-vk2 (k-split, ring 5). Five per (layer, m).

hypothesis.verification_done_offline: emu_pw10.py (scratchpad), the pw9 emulator generalized to the KSW warp mapping: per-warpgroup low-byte block and code-word selection, the escape register offset, and the summed k-split partials in staging. w1d8 (KS 2), w1d8z (odd m=121, KS 1), w2c2, wk2 (KS 2; and odd m=97, KS 1), vk2 (m=256), v2c2 (m=200) are bit-exact on one-hot rows and fp64-exact on random rows; the descriptor/swizzle address check passes. The release protocol is pw9's (630 simulated schedules, including 8 consumer warps); the wait_group(0) control releases each slot only after its own MMAs complete. Lint ok; cpu-check --official 9/9; full CUDA_SRC compiles with -std=c++20 against the torch mock with no warnings.

decision.reason: check 824f32ce203541c4: 9/9, 3385.7 us = r6 within run-to-run noise (CI 1.405-1.448 covers r6's 1.409); every gx path lost its bake to r6's own kernel by 1-3 us (q128a cluster +1.0 at m=1, q144b last-arriver +2.0; pooler p128b m=32 +3.2 vs kill rule of -1.5); 12-bit router paths +2.5 over r6's bf16 router. Wide-row tiles with cross-CTA split-K are dead in the r6 lineage too.

changes_vs_brief: Cluster dims stay r6's (1,1,KS) along grid z (the K-split index), not (1,KS,1): r6's escape lists, DSMEM rank math and launch already use z.
The router one-hot check compares against hi+lo, not the fp32 weight: a hi/lo BF16 pair cannot be bit-exact to fp32. This is what r6's _gvok does.
The (b) fences are fence.acq_rel.gpu, not __threadfence (fence.sc): MEMBAR.ALL.GPU instead of MEMBAR.SC.GPU.
The last arriver adds its own partial from shared memory and reads only the KS-1 peer slots from L2.
hypothesis.claim: r6's gv kernel is at the HBM stream at m=1 because it has no barrier between launch and the last load and no cross-CTA dependency. It loses at m>=16 because x is re-fetched once per 16-row tile: x traffic is (N/16)*m*K*2 B, 1.33x the 12-bit W bytes at m=16 and 2.67x at m=32. Fitted to r6's own kernels, L2->SM is about 7-7.5 TB/s, so W + x exceeds the HBM time at m=32. It also loses on qkv at every m: 144 CTAs on 132 SMs. pw11 keeps r6 byte-for-byte (all 78 r6 gv kernels have identical SASS; every r6 path is still baked and becomes the per-shape baseline 'r6') and adds gv geometries with 128-144 rows per CTA (x fetched once per 128 rows) and a 2/4/8-way cross-CTA K split. The split is reduced either by (a) r6's cluster DSMEM epilogue, guarded by cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters, or (b) a new no-cluster epilogue (V bit 2): fp32 partial with st.global.cg.v4 to a per-n-block slot, fence.acq_rel, atomicAdd counter, and the last arriver sums the others from L2 plus its own from smem, writes bf16 and resets the counter. Also: o at 64 rows with an x smem slab, and the router on the 12-bit codec for both hi and lo (6.3 MB instead of 8.4).

hypothesis.claim: The judge's probes put the cp.async.bulk stream at 4.15-4.4 TB/s, against 3.55-3.6 TB/s for register-direct ld.global (r6 pooler m=1 at 13.95 judge-us = 3.6 TB/s). That is about 2 us per 50 MB shape at m=1/8/16, where r6 is otherwise at its ceiling. The pw lineage lost that gain to a producer/consumer skeleton with cross-CTA split-K. pw12 keeps r6's gv kernel exactly (row tile per CTA, K split across the CTA's own warps, in-CTA smem reduction, same decode, mma, escapes and epilogue) and changes only how a warp gets its W bytes. Each warp streams its own contiguous K range through a PRIVATE smem ring of NS slots (4 or 8). Each slot is filled by one cp.async.bulk per row tile and matrix, of CU contiguous 1536 B chunks (CU = 1 or 2; r6's pack is contiguous per warp across chunks), issued by lane 0 on a per-slot mbarrier with expect_tx equal to the slot bytes. The warp try_waits its own barrier and reads the 3 x 16 B per lane with ld.shared.v4 at the offsets r6's ld.global.v4 used. After the slot's last chunk is decoded into registers: __syncwarp, then lane 0 issues fence.proxy.async and re-issues the slot. No producer warp, no cross-warp handshake, no named barrier in the loop. It is selected by V bit 3 (slot count in bits 4-5, chunks per slot in bits 6-7), so every r6 / pw11 geometry can take it. All pw11 paths are unchanged.

hypothesis.claim: The pw10 ladder split the 17 µs over the stream into four costs; see proj_rsi/audits/pw10-ladder.md. pw13 removes three of them on the m=128 / m=256 wgmma path. (1)+(iii): separate rings. W goes into a deep ring of its own (6 x 24 KB = 144 KB in flight at m=128) and is released right after the decode, so the HBM-bound W stream no longer waits for the MMA. x tiles go into a 4-slot ring released after the covering wgmma.wait_group. (iv): no cluster in the epilogue. fp32 partials are stored to a per-n-block workspace, then a fence and a counter; the last CTA reads the peers with .cg loads, transposes through smem and stores bf16 rows. (ii) is tried as a variant: x multicast to an n-block pair. Expected pooler m=128 about 25 µs in-prepare (torch 28.9; pw10 best 31.7).

design.consumer: Per chunk u: [u % CPW == 0: wait wfull] -> 3 LDS + pw_dec + escape XOR -> [last chunk of the W stage: arrive wempty] -> wait xfull(u) -> fence -> 4 wgmma (2 per warpgroup with the k-split) -> commit -> wait_group 1 -> pin A(u-1), arrive xempty(u-1) (multicast: also on the peer's xempty via mapa + mbarrier.arrive.release.cluster.shared::cluster). End: wait_group 0, release the last x slot. SASS order per stage: LDS, PRMT, W release, WARPGROUP.ARRIVE, 4 HGMMA, DEPBAR.LE gsb0 1, x release.
design.deviation: The brief asked for stmatrix from the D layout. I kept the scalar st.shared.u16 transpose that pw9/pw10 already validated on the judge, because an untested stmatrix .trans layout would have no offline check. It is off the critical path (16 KB once per n-block, after the stream).
design.epilogue: Consumer-only named barrier. D is staged in fragment order (k-split: the second warpgroup adds its D). For KS > 1, each CTA writes its partial (FRAG float4, coalesced) to ws[nb][ks], then __threadfence, barrier, one atomicAdd on cnt[nb]. A CTA that is not last returns. The last does __threadfence, adds the KS-1 peer partials with __ldcg, resets cnt[nb] = 0 (clean graph replays) and continues. Then fragment -> [token][row] bf16 transpose in smem (16 KB at m=128) and 16-B row stores (BN = 64 -> 128 B per token row). No workspace zeroing: partials are overwritten every call. No cluster.
design.k_split: hk2: 2 consumer warpgroups on the same 64 rows, k16 steps {0,1} / {2,3}, branch-free (no ptxas C7520), setmaxnreg 40 / 232. It sits on the new rings, m=128 only.
design.ks_rule: No rank rectangles any more, so KS = the largest of 1..4 with NB*KS <= 132: qkv 36 x 3 = 108, o 128 x 1, pooler 64 x 2, unpooler 128 x 1 (BN 64).
design.multicast: hmc / vhmc: cluster (2,1,1) along n (NB even for every layer). The tensor map box is NT/2 rows; CTA rank r multicasts rows [r*NT/2, (r+1)*NT/2) into both CTAs at the same smem offset (a 1024-aligned half, so the swizzle phase is unchanged). Each CTA's xfull expects the whole tile (both halves), and xempty counts both CTAs' consumer warps, so a slot is refilled only after both CTAs' wgmmas retired it. Cluster syncs sit after barrier init (before any multicast) and after the stream (no remote write or arrive after it). The epilogue is the same no-cluster one. x L2 traffic halves (64 MB at pooler m=128).
design.producer: One lane. Barrier init, the W prologue first (private), then the x prologue (after a cluster sync for multicast). Then a merged in-order schedule: issue whichever ring's next stage is needed at the earlier chunk (W stage w at chunk w*CPW, x stage s at chunk s), waiting on that ring's empty barrier. This order cannot deadlock: every x stage a pending W release depends on, and every W stage a pending x release depends on, is already issued. Checked in the protocol simulation.
design.rings: x ring: XST slots of the NT x 64 x tile (16 KB at m=128, 32 KB at m=256), TMA SWIZZLE_128B, xfull count 1 (expect_tx = whole tile), xempty count NWC (x 2 with multicast). W ring: WST slots of CPW = 4 chunks x RTB tiles x 1536 B (24 KB; a partial last stage carries fewer bytes), wfull count 1, wempty count NWC. m=128: XST 4, WST 6 (smem 209 KB); m=256: XST 3, WST 5 (217 KB). 1 CTA/SM.

probes.steps: L0 = r6's ld.global W stream only, consumed by an XOR into one register (no x, decode, mma, reduction or store). L1 = + x loads (XOR-consumed). The steps are V bits 9-11 of the same template, so everything else is r6's code.

hypothesis.question: What makes r6's gv about 3 us slower at m=32 than at m=1 (judge pooler 16.86 vs 13.91, qkv 14.76 vs 9.71), when pw11 showed x L2 traffic costs at most about 1 us? pw14 is pw12 unchanged (same bake, same PICK logic; every pw12 kernel's SASS is identical) plus a PROBE ladder on r6's own gv kernel. It reports, from the same _time_us, how the time builds up from the bare W stream to the full kernel at m=1/8 and m=32, plus two register-cap probes and the pw12 bulk ring's bare stream at m=32.
reading_guide: L0(m=32) vs L0(m=1): the W stream itself at the m=32 geometry (256 thr, 2 CTAs/SM) vs the m=1 geometry (1024 thr, 1 CTA/SM).
L1 - L0: x loads (L1/L2 traffic plus LSU wavefronts). pw11 bounds this at about 1 us.
L2 - L1: decode. It should not depend on m, since decode is shared by all token tiles.
L3 - L2: mma issue and latency, about 4x more HMMA at m=32 than at m=8.
L4 - L3: in-CTA reduction plus epilogue (qkv m=32 also includes the cluster-2 DSMEM step).
cap255 / cap64 vs L4: whether registers, through occupancy, limit bytes in flight.

decision.reason: check ce1163b9280c47a2: 9/9, 4423 us; kill rule hit: token-tiled paths pooler m=128 37.5-44.5 vs torch 30.5 (pw10's wk2 31.5 remains best). hypothesis.claim: Last m=128 experiment: drop split-K entirely. Every earlier m=128 epilogue cost 4-8 µs (cluster DSMEM reduce +4.5, global last-arriver +8.2) at the tail of a one-wave grid. cuBLAS avoids that for pooler by tiling over tokens as well as rows. pw15 adds that structure to pw10's best pipeline (single ring, release after the covering wait_group): each CTA owns 64 W rows x a 64-token tile over the full K, with token tiles of one n-block launched adjacently so the second read of each packed W chunk hits L2. There is no workspace, counter or cluster, and bf16 is written straight from the wgmma D layout. Pooler m=128 = 64 x 2 = 128 CTAs. The W stream (50 MB packed) is read once from HBM and once from L2; x per CTA is 64 tokens x full K.

design.epilogue: bf16 pairs from the D layout: even g stores rows (g, g+1) of token 2t, odd g rows (g-1, g) of token 2t+1, each a 32-bit word (one shfl.xor 4 exchanges partner values), plus the +8 rows. No transpose buffer, no partials. Every output element is written exactly once (checked in the emulator).
design.grid: 1-D, cta = nb * NTT + tt with NTT = ceil(m / TN); TMA box {64, TN} at token row tt*TN; rows >= m are zero-filled.
design.ping_pong: Warpgroup kg takes chunks kg, kg+2, ...; pw10's A double buffering per warpgroup over its own chunk sequence; the escape walk skips entries of the other warpgroup's chunks (pw_fix4; lists ascend by chunk). The launcher requires an even ST >= 4: with an odd ST a ring slot alternates owners, a warpgroup skips every other phase of its full barrier, and the parity wait aliases. The protocol simulation found this at ST 3 (decode of a refilled slot) and ST 2 (deadlock).
design.ring: pw10's single ring: stage = [x tile TN x 64][W chunk 4 x 1536 B], expect_tx = both, released after the wait_group covering the chunk. Empty barriers count the 4 warps of the warpgroup that owns the stage.

decision.reason: check f03e2e7785224172: 9/9, 3365 us = r6 within noise (CI 1.414-1.457). x cache policy exhausted: bypassing L1 (.cg) costs +2 to +9 us so r6 already gets substantial L1 reuse of x; evict_last ties r6 (qkv m=16 -0.5 within noise); forcing max L1 carveout costs +8 to +22. No path won a bake.

hypothesis.claim: pw14's ladder puts 2.5-2.8 us of r6's m=32 time on the x loads (pooler, qkv). r6's x loads are ld.global.nc.v4, which compile to LDG.E.128.CONSTANT: they already allocate in L1 with normal eviction, so the brief's option (a) ('allocate x in L1 instead of no_allocate') is r6's current state. Only W uses .L1::no_allocate. What is not known is whether r6 gets any L1 reuse of x: the 2 to 4 co-resident CTAs on an SM stream the same K order, and the driver chooses the L1/smem carveout. pw16 measures that on r6's own judge-picked m=16/32 geometries with zero structural change. Per shape there are four variants: x via ld.global.cg (L1 bypass: the cost of losing whatever reuse r6 has now), x with L1::evict_last (x kept against the no_allocate W stream), carveout 0 (largest L1 the kernel's smem allows), and evict_last + carveout 0. Options (b) and (c) were not built. (b) needs warps that share k: every r6 m=16/32 pick has WR=1 (warps split K), and r6's own WR=2 candidates lost by 0-1.3 us in its bake (pooler m=32 2.4.16.2: 17.3 vs 16.0). (c) is a cluster launch (about 1 us measured) for at most 1.3 us of saving.
hypothesis.kill_if: Kill the x-cache line if no pooler m=32 gc variant is at least 1.0 us under the 'r6' line in the same bake. Reading the result: if gc-*-xcg is no slower than r6, r6 gets no L1 reuse of x today; then if xel / L1 / xelL1 are also flat, the x cost is L1/LSU wavefronts and register depth, not L2 bytes, and the next lever is fewer x instructions per W byte (RT=2 with a register budget), not caching.

decision.reason: check 9f6de54218a447d5: 9/9 correct (codec E bit-exact on the judge) but every E path lost: pooler m=1 ge-p512r 26.24 vs r6 18.30 in-prepare, qkv m=1 26.34 vs 14.37, unpooler m=1 18.75 vs 8.77. hypothesis.claim: Codec E cuts r6's 12-bit W stream to 11.07 bits/weight on the reference weights. That figure includes per-lane padding, the LUT, the escape lists and the offsets; the code alone is 10.86. On the judge's weights it is a 7.8% byte cut on every m <= 16 shape that gv serves at the HBM stream. The decode is about 196 SASS per warp-chunk, 6.1 per weight, against r6's 49 on the same geometry. It should stay hidden at m <= 8, where r6 uses about 20% of issue and a 512-thread CTA keeps 16 decoding warps per SM, so pooler m=1 should fall by about 1.0-1.1 us of stream minus about 0.2 us for the 512-thread geometry. The format is a pair-Huffman code over the 8-bit exponent: <= 8 bits per A register, decoded with one 256-entry LUT (in smem) per mma A register, a per-lane 64-bit bit buffer, and a per-lane cp.async ring of 4 or 8 16-byte pieces. The sign|mantissa byte plane rides in r6's low-byte plane slots, and an 8-bit-XOR variant of r6's escape walk handles escapes. The A fragments, mma, reduction and epilogue are r6's own.
hypothesis.kill_if: pooler m=1 E path not ≥ 0.8 µs under r6 in the same bake
hypothesis.local_checks: Full gv block, 98 instances, compiled with nvcc 12.8 sm_90a -O3 in 27 s locally (r6 alone takes 14 s). r6's 78 instances are SASS-identical to r6-c12. The breakdown is 16 LUT LDS [R+UR], 4 ring LDS, 1 predicated LDGSTS + LDGDEPBAR + DEPBAR.LE SB0,2, 4 HMMA, and no LDL/STL. An instruction-level CPU emulation of the FMT-4 data path is bit-exact on the reference weights on every served geometry and variant. It covers generic PRMT/LOP3, the smem ring with early and late landing, the LUT smem image and the escape walk. It found and fixed the study's ce_sel immLut: 0xe4 must be 0xb8. lint ok; cpu-check --official 9/9; the CPU mock of the bake builds every plan.

hypothesis.claim: pw17's E paths ran at 1.45-2.1x the stream because each lane's decode was a serial chain through shared memory. The bake measured about 2,500 clk per unit per warp, against about 1,560 needed and about 800 estimated. Two causes stack: every pair's code length came from an LDS (about 110 clk effective per chained LDS), and the v2 lane-contiguous ring made each refill LDS 12-way (ED 4) or 22-way (ED 8) bank-conflicted, which explains why d8 was slower than single and single slower than rep (codec-study post-mortem). v3 makes three changes. (a) The code length is fixed by the first 3 bits (DP-optimal prefix code, +0.03 bits/weight against Huffman), so the bit-position chain per pair is LOP3, then PRMT, then SHF.R.W: three ALU ops with no memory. The value LUT LDS hangs off the chain and the compiler batches them. (b/c) There are 1, 2 or 4 independent substreams per lane. (d) The ring is [substream][slot][lane] with 4 B pieces, one bank per lane, so it is conflict-free, and refill words are prefetched one step ahead. Expected chain is about 16 x 3 ALU + 4 refills, about 300 clk per unit, so the kernel should run at the HBM stream for 11.07 bits (K1) and pooler m=1 should fall about 1 us below r6. The cost is issue: 256-286 SASS per unit against r6's 49, about 66% of issue at pooler m=1 with 16 warps/SM.

hypothesis.claim: Every pw m>=128 design lost to cuBLAS because one warpgroup paid stream wait, decode and MMA in turn per stage. pw19 ('tw') splits the CTA into a producer warp, a decode warpgroup and one or two MMA warpgroups. The producer feeds separate W and x rings, polls their empty barriers and is never blocked by MMA progress. The decode warpgroup writes bf16 A tiles into a third ring in the wgmma K-major 128B-swizzled layout, then fences the async proxy. The MMA warpgroups run SS wgmma (both operands through descriptors, no register A). On the budget, per 64-k stage at BN 64: stream about 420 clk; decode 330 warp-instr over 4 schedulers, hidden; tensor 256 clk at m=128 and 512 at m=256, so m=256 is tensor-bound at any BN; shared-memory traffic about 60 KB, about 470 clk at 128 B/clk, the binding limit at BN 64. BN 128 halves the x fills, to about 400 clk per 64 rows. Expected pooler m=128 in-prepare: t64 about 27-29 against cuBLAS 29.4 (W+x 25 + epilogue 4.5, decode and MMA hidden). A 3-4 us win, if any, comes from t128 (BN 128, cluster 4, 128 CTAs) or t64x2 (2 CTAs/SM, 256 CTAs, twice the bytes in flight).

changes_from_pw1: Grid is now (NG n-groups, KS K-slices) and each CTA walks a range of n-blocks; pw1 was (NB, KS) with one n-block per CTA.
x is copied into smem once per CTA with cp.async (rows >= m zero-filled), no longer as one bulk copy per row per stage through the mbarrier ring.
The ring engine has no producer warp and no barrier at all; its cursor crosses n-block boundaries without draining. The bulk engine's producer streams W only, in 12-24 KB stages.
Partial reductions are issued per finished n-block inside the stream. Arrival counting and last-arriver finalization run once at the end over the CTA's n-blocks (a CTA may finalize several).
Escape entry format widened to a 15-bit step field (seq<<17) over the whole n-range walk.

Instance set: 8-warp CTAs everywhere (BN=128 except rm BN=64), ring D=4 and D=8 at every small m, m=128 BN=128 bulk with 12 KB and 24 KB stages, and an m=128 ring. 12 GEMM instantiations plus 6 small probe kernels, one PATHS entry each (12 paths, down from 22).
Grid chooser: smem-feasible (x slice + W ring), one wave (two for small m <= 8 jobs), minimizing x re-read + 2x reductions.
New PROBE section in prepare() and a pw_probe glue entry point. A PW build line per path and shape logs NG/KS/grid/x-slice KB.
hypothesis.claim: pw1 was correct on all 120 builds but slow. Its x went through the shared-memory ring as one bulk copy per token row per 64-k stage, with a producer/consumer mbarrier round trip each stage, so the cost scaled with m and even m=1 streamed W at only about 2.7 TB/s. pw2 keeps the codec, fragment maps and self-cleaning epilogue and changes only the data flow. Each CTA owns a K-slice and a range of n-blocks. It copies x[:, K-slice] into shared memory once (cp.async, overlapped with the first W loads), then streams a long range of W (100-400 KB per CTA) through an engine that knows nothing about x: a barrier-free per-warp register ring (D=4 or 8), or a W-only bulk ring of 12-24 KB stages. Finished n-blocks reduce with red.global.add.v4.f32 and arrival counting happens once at the end. Small m should then stream at the engine's own rate (the PROBE lines measure it: target >= 4 TB/s on packed bytes, which puts pooler m=1 near 12.5 us + ~4 us graph cost in prepare terms). m=16/32 should no longer be 2x slower than m=1. m=128 loses the 128-copies-per-stage handshake, which was the main cost (pw1 159 us vs 30 us torch in prepare).

The full CUDA_SRC compiles with -std=c++20 against a minimal torch mock; the local torch wheel lacks the CUDA c10 headers, so the real glue was compiled only on the judge for pw1.

design.engines: MODE 0 ring: each consumer warp keeps D (4 or 8) chunks x RT tiles x 3 x 16 B in flight with ld.global.nc.L1::no_allocate.v4 (L1-allocating ld.global.nc when WTOK = 2 warps share a unit). There is no producer warp and no barrier in the main loop, and the cursor walks (n-block, chunk) across n-block boundaries without draining. MODE 1 bulk: the producer warp streams W only, CPS*BN rows per stage (12 KB at CPS=1, 24 KB at CPS=2), ST deep; full/empty mbarriers guard W only.
design.epilogue: As in pw1. After each n-block, KS == 1 stores bf16 straight from registers; otherwise red.global.add.v4.f32 per fragment (only lanes holding a valid token) into the fragment-ordered fp32 workspace, and acc is zeroed. After the whole stream: __threadfence, one atomicAdd per owned n-block, and the CTA collects the n-blocks it finished last (static list of <= 256). It then __threadfence's, converts with __ldcg, stores bf16, re-zeroes with __stcg, and resets the counter. There is no sync inside the stream.
design.escapes: As in pw1 (the r6 codec's escape list), but the entry is now seq<<17 | lane<<12 | reg<<8 | half<<7 | xor7. seq = (warp step i = (nb - nb0)*KCS + u) * RT + j, which runs across the CTA's whole n-range. The 15-bit field is checked < 32000 on the host and in the launcher.
design.grid: Grid (NG, KS). CTA (ng, ks) owns n-blocks [ng*NB/NG, (ng+1)*NB/NG) and K stages [ks*NST/KS, (ks+1)*NST/KS); both splits may be uneven. _pw_grid fits the x slice (TOK x (KCSmax*128+16) B) plus the W ring into 220 KB / CTAs-per-SM. It targets one wave (132 x CTAs/SM), or two waves for m <= 8 jobs under 16 MB of packed W. Among grids filling >= 85% of the target it minimizes x re-read NG*m*K*2 + 2*KS*m*N*4 (reductions weighted 2x; none when KS == 1).

design.m128_layout: bm12 / bm24: BN=128 (8 row tiles per chunk), 8 consumer warps = 4 (2 row tiles each) x 2 (64 tokens each). Accumulators 2 x 8 x 4 = 64 regs. Each A fragment is reused across 8 token tiles and each B fragment across 2 row tiles. W lives in the smem ring (12 KB x 6 or 24 KB x 3 stages) next to an x slice of at most about 146 KB; 1 CTA/SM. rm: register ring at m=128, BN=64, 8 warps = 4 x (1 row tile) x 2 (64 tokens), acc 32, D=4. The 2-row-tile ring version needed 255 regs and spilled, and so did a 16-warp version capped at 128.
design.register_budget_ptxas: nvcc 12.8 sm_90a -O3, every kernel 0 bytes stack and 0 spill. GEMM: r8t1d4 114, r8t1d8 159, b8t1 60, r8t2d4 118, r8t2d8 167, b8t2 66, r8t4d4 128, r8t4d8 200, b8t4 92, bm12 148, bm24 156, rm 206. Probes: ring D4 32, D8 48, D16 94, bulk 22, red 16, empty 10.
design.x_stationary: At kernel start every thread issues cp.async 16 B copies of x[:, K-slice] into the padded smem slice (row stride KCSmax*128+16, conflict-free B-fragment loads). Rows >= m are zero-filled through the cp.async src-size. The column of W chunk c is (c*64) % K, which is the K-wrap hook for the router. Then one wait_all + __syncthreads, and x is never touched again. The ring prologue loads (and the bulk producer's first ST stages) are issued before the x copy, so they overlap it.

probe.use: Calibrates the engines independently of decode/mma: if the GEMM paths lose again, these say whether the stream or the compute side is short, and which (D, warps, CTAs/SM) or (stage, ST) the next kernel should use.

risks: A hang or fault still cannot be caught by the bake-off. The new mbarrier logic is W-only and follows pw1's pipeline, which ran on the judge (init + prologue by the producer before __syncthreads; parity waits unchanged). The launcher range-checks NG, KS, the x row stride, the smem size, the escape-step bound and the workspace/counter/offset sizes, and falls back on any error.
m=128: the x-slice smem cap forces KS >= 15 on pooler, so the fp32 reductions are about 32 MB. If L2 reductions run at only ~3-5 TB/s that alone is 6-10 us; PROBE red reports it.
Small m with 1 CTA/SM (D=8 and bulk) gives 8 warps/SM. If latency hiding needs more warps, the D=4 2-CTA/SM ring variants and the PROBE table show it.
Uneven K splits mean some CTAs stream 1 chunk more than others (up to 1/KCS imbalance).
Log size: about 60 PW build lines + about 150 BAKE/PICK + 35 PROBE lines, estimated at 11 KB, under the 14 KB budget.

hypothesis.claim: qkv_gate's m <= 32 excess over the judge's speed-of-light (m=1 9.97 vs 8.42, m=16 11.36 vs 7.93) is geometry: r6 runs 144 one-tile CTAs on 132 SMs, so 12 SMs carry two tiles (max/mean 1.83). pw28 keeps r6's gv loop (12-bit dec1, register W ring, x in registers or through L1, escape walk, mma.sync with W as A) but cuts the 144 x 128 (tile, chunk) units into 128 equal CTA ranges of 144 units (9 warps x 16 or 18 warps x 8; max/mean 1.03; 4 SMs idle). A CTA runs its tile-B units first; at that switch step each warp stores its fp32 partial of a tile continued by the next CTA to its own workspace slot (st.relaxed.gpu, no fence, counter or barrier); the next CTA reads the slots at its end with ld.relaxed.gpu, re-reading while a word still holds the sentinel, restores the sentinel, and adds them in a fixed order (deterministic). In the interleaved order (V bit 4) the published part is finished early in time, so the end-of-kernel cost is one L2 read, not pw11's store-fence-atomic-load chain. 112 of 144 tiles have two contributors; slot traffic 0.5 MB (m<=8) to 2 MB (m=32), all L2.

hypothesis.claim: Two measurements and one m=128 design. (A) pw2's b8t1 took about 19 kernel-µs on pooler m=1, against 12.5 µs for the same bytes through a pure bulk stream. This check decomposes that 6.5 µs. The same bulk kernel is run with its consumer work switched on step by step (wait/arrive only, then smem loads, then decode, then mma without escapes, then full), in three CTA shapes and with one-arrive-per-two-stages. The next design can then target the stage that costs time, not a guess. (B) At m=128, split-K reductions cost about 0.8 µs per 2 MB on this judge, so KS must stay at or below 4 and x cannot be stationary. Instead each 64-k stage carries ONE 2D TMA copy of the x tile [128 x 64] (16 KB, 128B-swizzled) plus the 12 KB W chunk on the same full barrier: 28 KB stages, 6 deep, 1 CTA/SM, BN=128. Compute is mma.sync at about 1.6 clk per m16n8k16 per SM (about 13 µs for pooler); the stream is 50 MB at 3.8 TB/s (13 µs); 8 MB of reductions (about 3 µs, partly overlapped). That points to pooler m=128 near 16-18 kernel-µs, against cuBLAS's ~25 kernel-µs (30.1 in prepare).

m128_design.graph_safety_note: The brief's worry was that a host-encoded map would be stale on a graph replay with new x. Every kernel argument, including the plain x pointer that pw1 and pw2 already pass (and that passed their timed-correctness checks), is frozen at capture time. So the judge necessarily refills the captured x storage on every replay, and a map baked into the parameters is exactly as valid as the raw pointer. pw-tms implements the requested staging variant anyway (x copied into a buffer allocated in build, then the map is encoded over that fixed address), at about 1 µs of extra D2D copy. The bake-off decides between them on speed, and both are validated.
m128_design.grid_and_split: Grid (NB = N/128, KS). tm: KS = clamp(round(132/NB), 1, 4): qkv 18x4 = 72 CTAs, o 64x2 = 128, pooler 32x4 = 128, unpooler 64x2 = 128. Reductions 4.7 / 8.4 / 8.4 / 8.4 MB, at most about 3.4 µs at the probed 2.5 TB/s. tmh: KS halved: qkv 2, o 1, pooler 2, unpooler 1, so o and unpooler have no reductions at half a wave of CTAs. This is the reduction-vs-occupancy trade-off measured directly.
m128_design.kernel: pwt<RT=2, WN=4, WTOK=2, TTW=8, ST=6>, 8 consumer warps + 1 producer warp (288 threads), 150 regs, 1 CTA/SM. Smem: 1024 B alignment pad + 6 x 28672 B stages + barriers = 173 KB.
m128_design.stage: 28 KB stage: [x tile 128 rows x 64 k, 16 KB, 128B-swizzled TMA box at coordinates (k = (chunk*64) % K, row 0)][W chunk 8 tiles x 1536 B = 12 KB, cp.async.bulk]. One full barrier per stage with expect_tx = 16384 + 12288. Rows >= m are zero-filled by the TMA out-of-bounds fill (the map uses the exact m), so expect_tx is always the full box.
m128_design.tensor_map: cuTensorMapEncodeTiled, fetched once through cudaGetDriverEntryPoint (no -lcuda): bf16, dims {K, m}, stride K*2, box {64, 128}, SWIZZLE_128B, L2 promotion 128B, OOB fill zero. pw-tm/pw-tmh encode it on the host on every call for that call's x pointer and pass it as a __grid_constant__ kernel parameter (alignas(64) 128-byte struct). The kernel hands its generic address to cp.async.bulk.tensor.2d.
m128_design.warp_layout: Warp (wn, wt) owns row tiles 2wn, 2wn+1 and tokens 64wt..64wt+63 (8 n8 tiles). Accumulators 2 x 8 x 4 = 64 regs. Each decoded A fragment is reused across 8 token tiles and each B fragment across 2 row tiles. B fragment loads read row R = 64wt + 8tt + g at R*128 + (((2t)^g)<<4) and (((2t+1)^g)<<4), which matches the swizzle (chunk ^ (row & 7)) and is conflict-free.

configs.c16w1: 16 consumer warps (BN 256), 24 KB stages of 1 chunk x 16 tiles, so each warp owns 1 unit per stage instead of 2. ST 4, 1 CTA/SM, pooler grid 16x8 = 128.
configs.c8w1: 8 consumer warps (BN 128, 1 tile per warp), 24 KB stages (CPS 2), ST 4, 1 CTA/SM. This is the shipped shape. Pooler grid 18x7 = 126.
configs.c8w1 AG2: The L5 c8w1 kernel with one empty-barrier arrive per 2 stages (paired slots): the handshake cost.
configs.c8w2: Same instantiation with ST 2 (half the ring) and the grid sized for 2 CTAs/SM: 26x10 = 260, smem 62 KB (m=1) / 105 KB (m=32). Tests whether more resident warps hide the consumer.

levels.L1: Producer streams W exactly as in the path; consumers only wait(full) and arrive(empty), no smem reads. Stream + handshake + x-slice load + epilogue cost.
levels.L2: + the 3 x 16 B ld.shared per unit per warp, XOR-consumed into a register stored at the end: smem read bandwidth/latency of the W stage.
levels.L3: + the 12-bit decode (pw_unit, 16 prmt-based registers per unit) XOR-consumed: ALU cost of decode.
levels.L4: + the B-fragment loads and mma.sync for all token tiles, with pw_fix compiled out (results wrong, timed only): tensor-core issue and B traffic.
levels.L5: the full path (= b8t1 at m=1, b8t4 at m=32), adding the escape walk.

risks: TMA tensor-map path is new to this candidate family (r7's encode was the 2D no-swizzle form via -lcuda). If cudaGetDriverEntryPoint or the encode fails, pw_run_tma returns a code, run() falls back, and the BAKE line still validates (it measures the fallback). A wrong swizzle assumption shows up as INVALID, not a crash. A hang is possible only if expect_tx disagreed with the bytes delivered: the TMA always delivers the full box (16384) and the bulk copy 12288, matching expect_tx.

hypothesis.verification_done_offline: emu_pw3.py (scratchpad). (1) Emulates pwt end to end: TMA box placement with the 128B swizzle at the stage's k coordinate (rows >= m zero), W chunk after the 16 KB x tile, decode, escape walk, swizzled B-fragment reads (it asserts no unwritten byte is read), fragments, split-K flush, finalize, and workspace/counters back to zero. 3 geometries are bit-exact on one-hot rows and fp64-exact on random rows: uneven KS=3, KS=1 with m=121, KS=2. (2) A randomized-schedule simulation of the mbarrier protocols (pwk with ST 2/4/6/8, NSTOT 1-32, AG 1/2; pwt with ST 2/6, KCS 1-32): 30 schedules each, no deadlock, no read before fill, no overwrite before release. Mutating the producer's parity or the AG2 release slot is caught. The pwk address math is unchanged from pw2, whose emulator passed and whose 120+ builds validated on the judge.

hypothesis.claim: CUTLASS bf16 parity configs transfer to the H200. A 233-config H100 sweep (proj_rsi/tools/cutlass_sweep.py, proj_rsi/audits/cutlass_sweep.md) found four basic warp-specialised instantiations that cover the big-four shapes at m = 128 / 256 within ~1% of torch on the box (geomean 1.009 vs best torch): c64n = swap-AB 64x64x64 cluster 1x2 no-smem epilogue (qkv / pooler m=128), c128 = swap-AB 128x128x64 cluster 1x2 (o / unpooler m=256), n128 = non-swapped 64x128x64 raster along W rows (pooler m=256, unpooler / o m=128), n96 = non-swapped 64x96x64 raster along W rows (qkv m=256, 96 tiles like nvjet's 96x64). pw30 = pw26 with exactly these four; each is baked on all eight (layer, m) shapes against r6 (r6's own m=128/256 choice is tuned cuBLASLt) and picked per shape.
hypothesis.expected: Score-neutral (all picks r6 on the H100); information value only: whether the H200 bake reproduces the H100 ordering and the c64n gap to r6 at pooler m=128.

H100 (/root/bench.sh pw30 --official): all official CHECKs ok; cut compiled in 58 s; PREPARE 94.8 s. H100 bake (us, r6 = tuned cuBLASLt / cuBLASLt heuristic / best CUTLASS): qkv128 18.82/20.38/c64n 21.15; qkv256 21.47/23.20/n96 22.94; o128 10.78/10.88/n128 11.10; o256 11.62/11.97/c128 12.13; pooler128 27.42/28.61/c64n 28.26; pooler256 29.44/36.93/n128 30.82; unpooler128 26.88/28.16/n128 28.26; unpooler256 28.06/30.24/c128 30.34. The per-shape ranking of the four matches the sweep, and they sit at about cuBLASLt-heuristic (torch) parity, but r6's tuned cuBLASLt beats every one by 0.3-2.3 us, so on the H100 every PICK is r6.
hypothesis.mechanics: Same embedded CUTLASS 3.9.2 header bundle as pw26 (no new headers needed: the new CUTCU compiles against the extracted bundle alone). C is void (beta = 0). StageCountAutoCarveout, PersistentScheduler with runtime raster order, hw_info.sm_count cached. load_inline 'cut30_*' with CUTFLAGS incl. -DNDEBUG and -gencode=arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a.

hypothesis.claim: pw3 showed the compute is nearly hidden (L5 full only 1.3-2.3 µs above the L1 wait/arrive skeleton). The skeleton itself is 4-5 µs slower than a pure bulk stream of the same 50 MB at m=1, and about 5 µs slower again at m=32 with identical W bytes. pw4 names those microseconds with one-change-per-line probes on the L1 skeleton (16 consumer warps, pooler, m=1 and m=32). In the same check it measures the likely fixes on the real paths: the producer issues its first W stages before any other prologue work and exits when done; the split-K epilogue runs on the consumer warps only behind a named barrier; the escape-list loads are issued before the x copy. Prediction: the x-slice prologue is the dominant term, about 1 µs at m=1 and 3-4 µs at m=32. Its 66 KB per CTA is copied by all threads before any consumer starts, and the W ring stalls once its 4 stages are full. If nopro/xreg confirm that, the next design overlaps the x copy with consumption (per-chunk x readiness) instead of front-loading it.

fixes_applied.a_consumer_only_epilogue: The end-of-CTA arrival counting and last-arriver finalize (pw_arrive) now synchronise only the consumer warps (bar.sync 1, NWC*32). The producer warp returns right after its last issue, in pwk and pwt. Note: pwk's per-n-block flush never had a __syncthreads (it is fire-and-forget red.v4), so the producer was never blocked mid-stream by the epilogue. The only CTA-wide barrier left is the one after the prologue. Expected gain is small (the producer no longer joins the final barrier).
fixes_applied.b_w_first: pwk already issued the first ST W stages from the producer thread before the x copy (since pw2). pwt (m=128) now does the same: barrier init + first ST stages (x TMA tile + W chunk each) before the CTA sync, and the loop starts at stage ST.
fixes_applied.c_escape_prefetch: The eoff / first esc loads are issued before the x copy, in pwk and pwt, so their two dependent global loads overlap the prologue instead of following the CTA sync.
fixes_applied.correctness: PRB (probe switches) is a template flag; the GEMM instances compile with PRB=0, where the launcher also rejects non-zero probe fields. Named-barrier count = consumer threads exactly (warps 0..NWC-1 are the consumers); the producer never takes part. The randomized protocol simulation covers the producer exiting early with a consumer-only final barrier, the prologue issued before the sync (pwk, pwt) or after it (LATE), FREE per-stage barriers, and two copies per stage (pwt). No deadlock, no read before fill, no overwrite before release in any schedule; a producer that skips its empty wait is caught in 20/20 runs.
fixes_applied.extra_paths: pw-b16t1 / b16t2 / b16t4 (16 consumer warps, BN 256, 24 KB stages) added beside the 8-warp paths, because pw3's probes had 16 warps 0.8-2.7 µs faster at L5. Existing paths are unchanged apart from the fixes. pw-tmh (parked in LOOP.md) removed; pw-tm and pw-tms kept.

hypothesis.claim: pw4 located the whole skeleton gap in the epilogue: noepi saves 2.3 µs at m=1 and 5.2 µs at m=32 against base, and noepi+nopro sits at the pure stream. pw5 splits that epilogue into its parts with probes (reductions, fence, counter, finalize, vector width, fence scope). It also moves the epilogue off the critical path on the real m<=32 paths. Two extra epilogue warps take each finished n-block from a double-buffered smem staging area and reduce, fence, count and finalize it while the 16 consumer warps stream the next n-block. That needs at least 2 n-blocks per CTA. pw4's grid gave pooler exactly 1 (NG = NB = 16 at BN 256), so the overlapped paths are registered at >= 2 and >= 4 n-blocks per CTA. Only the last n-block's epilogue stays exposed. Prediction: the overlapped skeleton lands within ~1 µs of noepi at both m. With compute nearly hidden (pw3), the full GEMM then lands ~1.5-2 µs above pure, about 13.5-14 judge µs at m=1/16/32 on pooler and qkv.

epilogue_design.barriers: mbarriers sfull[2] (count 16, one arrive per consumer warp after __syncwarp) and sempty[2] (count EW). A consumer finishing n-block i (i-th of its CTA) waits sempty[i&1] with parity ((i>>1)-1)&1 when i >= 2. It then st.shared.v4's its fragments into buffer i&1, zeroes its accumulators, arrives sfull[i&1], and continues streaming. Epilogue warp loop i = 0..NBR-1: wait sfull[i&1] with parity (i>>1)&1, read the fragments (ld.shared.v4), arrive sempty[i&1] (the buffer is free as soon as it is read), then the proven split-K ordering: red.global.add.v4 -> per-thread __threadfence -> epilogue-only named barrier (bar.sync 2, 64) -> one atomicAdd on cnt[nb] -> bar.sync 2 -> if last: __threadfence, batched ld.cg / st.cg zero / bf16 store of the n-block (8 loads in flight per thread), cnt[nb] = 0. KS == 1: the epilogue warps convert and store bf16 from smem directly, with no reductions or counters.
epilogue_design.buffers: Two staging buffers of FRAG = RTB*TT*32 float4 in fragment order (identical to the workspace layout): 8 KB each at m<=8, 16 KB at m=16, 32 KB at m=32. They sit between the W ring + barriers and the x slice. smem per CTA (pooler): 128 KB (m<=8, ring 4 x 24 KB), 146-160 KB (m=16, ring 4), 157-201 KB (m=32, ring dropped to 3). The grid chooser and the launcher include the staging bytes.
epilogue_design.exit_order: The producer exits after its last issue. The consumers exit after parking their last n-block (no CTA-wide barrier after the prologue). The epilogue warps exit last, after the last n-block's count/finalize, so only that n-block's epilogue is exposed.
epilogue_design.grid: Overlapped paths use _pw_grid(..., nbr_min): NG <= NB/nbr_min. pw-b16t* use nbr_min 2 and pw-b16t*n4 use 4 (pooler 8x15 and 4x29; qkv 4x29 and 2x57; unpooler 16x8 / 8x15 at m >= 16). Reductions rise with KS: m=32 pooler 7.9 MB at nbr 2, 15.2 MB at nbr 4.
epilogue_design.m128: Left as in pw4. The tm kernel has one n-block per CTA (grid NB x KS), so an overlapped epilogue would have nothing after it to hide behind; only a multi-n-block tm grid would benefit, which is a different design.
epilogue_design.unchanged: Codec, fragment maps, escapes, x-stationary prologue, producer first-issue and escape prefetch (pw4). Probe switches are compiled only into the PRB=1 probe instances; the path instances reject non-zero flags.
epilogue_design.warps: Per CTA: warps 0-15 consumers (16 x 1 row tile of BN 256), warp 16 producer, warps 17-18 epilogue (EW = 2): 608 threads. ptxas: b16t1 69, b16t2 86, b16t4 89 regs, 0 spill, so 1 CTA/SM fits in registers.

Kill the whole m<=32 bulk family if pw-b16t* still loses to torch on pooler m=1 and m=32 after the overlap. r6 then keeps m<=32.

hypothesis.claim: Two things. (A) Whether the judge's 'yours' minus profiled kernel time (≈0 for r6's zero-smem gv kernels, +2.5-3.5 µs for ours at m=1, +1.5-4.9 for nvjet, +6.8 for the FP32 xmma) is an L1/shared-memory carveout reconfiguration at launch. The flush kernel (torch.sum) runs with little or no shared memory, so a following kernel that opts into a large dynamic smem forces the SM to re-partition L1/smem first. The carve probes measure that directly, with no memory traffic (empty kernels) and on a stream (bulk ring sizes, unused smem on a ring kernel, our own flush with and without smem). (B) pw5 showed the last-arriver finalize (ld.cg read-back from L2) is the bulk of the epilogue (3.8 of 5.8 µs at m=32). pw6 removes the global workspace entirely on the m<=32 paths. The K-split CTAs of one n-block form a cluster, park their partials in their own drained W-ring smem, and after one cluster barrier each rank sums its own row-tile slice from all peers over DSMEM and stores bf16. A second cluster barrier keeps peers' smem alive. There are no global reductions, fences, counters, finalize or zeroing. Predicted pooler m=32 epilogue: ~1 µs (one cluster barrier pair + 32 KB of DSMEM reads per CTA) instead of 5.8, i.e. the full path near pw4's noepi + ~1.5.

cluster_design.epilogue: After the K loop the producer warp does not exit; it joins a CTA-wide __syncthreads. At that point every consumer has passed its last full-barrier wait, so every W bulk copy has landed and been read, and the producer has issued its last stage. The W ring area is then free. The consumers store their fp32 accumulators (fragment order, all lanes; 8 KB at m<=8, 16 KB at m=16, 32 KB at m=32; ring >= 96 KB) at sbase + idx*16 with st.shared.v4. Then barrier.cluster.arrive.release + wait.acquire. Rank r owns fragments [r*FRAG/KS, (r+1)*FRAG/KS), which are row tiles [r*16/KS, (r+1)*16/KS) because fragments are tile-major. All 544 threads take an index each; for valid tokens (tok < m) they issue all KS mapa.shared::cluster + ld.shared::cluster.v4.f32 loads (peers 0..KS-1) before the adds, then store bf16. Finally a second cluster arrive/wait so no CTA exits while a peer still reads its smem. KS == 1: direct bf16 store from registers, no cluster launch.
cluster_design.grid: (NB, KS) with one BN=256 n-block per CTA, launched with cudaLaunchKernelEx and cudaLaunchAttributeClusterDimension (1, KS, 1), so a cluster is the KS K-split CTAs of one n-block and cluster_ctarank = blockIdx.y. KS = the largest of {8, 4, 2, 1} with NB*KS <= 132, KS <= K/64 and dividing the 16 row tiles, whose x slice + W ring fits. Grids: pooler 16x8 = 128, qkv 9x8 = 72, o 32x4 = 128, unpooler (m>=16) 32x4 = 128, unpooler n=1024 4x8 = 32 (b16) / 8x8 = 64 (b8t1c). smem 100-161 KB, 1 CTA/SM.

cluster_design.launch_guard: The launcher checks NG == NB, KS <= 8, KS | 16 and staging <= ring bytes. It calls cudaOccupancyMaxActiveClusters once per (KS, smem), caching up to 8 entries so graph capture does not repeat it, and returns -9 when it reports 0 or fails. cudaLaunchKernelEx errors are returned as codes. Any code makes run() use the fallback, so a cluster that cannot be placed declines instead of failing.

changes_from_pw6: New kernel pwc<RT, WN, WTOK, TTW, CPS, ST, CLU, MINB> replaces pwk for every m<=32 path. pwk's probe-era switches (LV, AG, PRB flags, byte-sized stages) are gone; the cluster and global epilogues are carried over unchanged.

(1) ST is a template parameter (4). The cluster stage loop is unrolled by ST with `if (s0 + k >= NSTOT) break;`. W base wl = sbase + wn*RT*1536 + lane*16 and x base are hoisted; barrier/W/x offsets are immediates; the phase flips once per outer iteration. The global path keeps a non-unrolled stage loop (register cap, see sass_before_after.not_reached).

(2) Chunk-major x slice [chunk][row][144 B]: the prologue copy writes it, and B fragments are read at xl + chunk*TOK*144 + tt*8*144 (+16) with immediate tile offsets. Bank groups (g + 2t) mod 8 are distinct per quarter-warp (checked for TOK 8/16/32/128). x fragments are loaded before pw_mbwait for all instances except the global m=32 one (loaded after the wait there, register cap). The x-slice smem is KCSmax*TOK*144 B (was TOK*(KCSmax*128+16)), accounted for in the grid choosers and the launcher.

(3) Escape compare against a loop-carried nxs = nx >> 17 (updated only on the hit path), with seq = (stage*CPS + cc)*RT + j (equal to pw6's ((cnb-nb0)*KCS+u)*RT + j). No per-chunk n-block boundary test in the cluster path. The launcher requires NG == NB for every cluster launch, including KS = 1, which flushes after the loop.
(4) Empty-barrier arrive right after pw_unit, before pw_fix and the mma (W smem is dead after the decode; x lives outside the ring).
(5) lane pinned with asm volatile("" : "+r"(lane)); p.Tb hoisted into a pinned register.
(6) New cluster paths pw-r2t2c (m=16: RT=2, WN=8, WTOK=2, TTW=1) and pw-r2t4c (m=32: RT=2, WN=8, WTOK=2, TTW=2). Same BN=256 n-block and pack layout as the b16 paths, 16 consumer warps.

hypothesis.claim: pw6 with the SASS audit's numerics-preserving edits applied to the m<=32 bulk kernel, rewritten as pwc. Statically measured on the cluster instances, the consumer hot path per 64-k chunk per warp drops 111 -> 84.25 instructions at m=32 (-24%), 90 -> 68.75 at m=1 (-24%) and 99 -> 75.75 at m=16. The x fragments are now loaded before the full-barrier wait, and the ring slot is released right after the decode instead of after the mma. The new RT=2 cluster shape (two W row tiles per warp sharing one x fragment set) halves the x shared-memory reads per W unit: 8 -> 4 LDS per W unit at m=32, the read bandwidth the audit found closest to binding (54%). Its cost is 62.9 instructions per W unit at m=32. Results are bit-identical to pw6 (same per-accumulator mma sequence). pw6's probe section is kept unchanged.

hypothesis.rt2_bit_identity: Each accumulator acc[j][tt] receives the same sequence of mma.sync operations as in RT=1: chunks in ascending order, k16 steps q = 0..3 within a chunk, with the same decoded A registers and the same B fragments. RT=2 only changes which warp owns which row tile and token tile. The fp32 rounding sequence per output element is therefore identical. The emulator confirms equal outputs for RT=1 and RT=2 at m=16 and m=32 on the same weights and grid.

sass_before_after.method: nvcc 12.8 -arch=sm_90a -cubin -O3, cuobjdump -sass, then a static hot-path walk of the consumer main loop (scratchpad sasscount.py). The walk runs from the header of the smallest backward branch containing all HMMAs to that back-edge. Conditional forward branches inside the loop that skip no HMMA are taken (escape bodies, n-block flushes); branches leaving the loop, going backward (spin retries, escape reloads) or skipping HMMAs (unrolled-loop breaks) are not. The count is divided by the chunks per loop iteration (pw6: 1; pw7 cluster: ST = 4; pw7 global: 1). It reproduces the audit's pw6 numbers exactly (111 / 90, class by class). Instructions per 64-k chunk per warp.
sass_before_after.not_reached: The audit's ~80 (m=32) / ~62 (m=1) targets were missed by about 4-7 instructions. The S2R/LDC remnants (2-3 per chunk: the escape list pointer and the ub/stage index) and the per-chunk break test of the unrolled loop remain. The global instance (b16t4g) keeps a non-unrolled loop and loads x after the wait: its ST-unrolled flush and an x prefetch both exceed the 96-register cap of a 17-warp CTA (8-16 B of spill), so it gets only the hoisting/escape/arrive edits (106 -> 95).
sass_before_after.order_check: pw7 m=32 cluster loop order in the SASS: 8 x LDS -> TRYWAIT -> 3 W LDS -> 16 PRMT (decode) -> ARRIVE -> HMMAs. The x loads precede the wait and the slot is released before any HMMA.

hypothesis.claim: pw7 plus the router as one packed tensor-core GEMM. W (fp32 [256, 8192]) runs as the BF16 hi + lo pair the rules allow: hi = bf16(W), lo = bf16(W - hi). Each part is packed with the same proven 12-bit codec (its own window base and escapes) and laid out as one contiguous range per n-block, [n-block][hi chunks 0..127, lo chunks 128..255][tile][1536]. The kernel treats the router as a K' = 2K = 16384 GEMM: x is read at chunk c % 128 (the K-wrap hook), the decode base switches to lo's at chunk 128, and accumulation and output are fp32. The router is 6.3 MB packed (vs 8.4 MB fp32 for r6's m<=8 kernel) and latency-bound, so it uses small CTAs: BN = 32 (2 consumer warps), 3 KB stages, 8 deep. Either cluster split-K (8 x 8 = 64 CTAs, DSMEM reduce) or the global epilogue (8 x 16 = 128 or 8 x 32 = 256 CTAs; the finalize read-back is at most 32 KB at m=32). At m=128 a 4-consumer-warp tile (2 x 64 tokens) with the global epilogue runs 8 x 32 = 256 CTAs. Target: <= 3.6 judge-µs at m <= 32 (r6: 4.1 / 5.1 / 5.9 / 5.1 at m = 1 / 8 / 16 / 32) and <= 5.0 at m=128 (r6 10.3, three kernels).

router_design.kernel: pwc<..., RTR = 1>: W chunks 0..255 of the n-block, x chunk = c % (K/64) (the x copy reads column (c*64) % K), decode base Tb for c < 128 and Tb2 for c >= 128 (one select per chunk, compiled only into RTR instances), fp32 output through pw_putp (runtime p.of, outside the hot loop). The launcher rejects RTR/of mismatches; the tm launcher rejects fp32 outputs.
router_design.packs: _c12(_pack(hi)) and _c12(_pack(lo)), each proven exact by _unc12 on its own, concatenated along the chunk dimension. lo's escapes are shifted by K/64 = 128 chunks. Real router weights (seed 5151): both packs exact, window bases 54 (hi) / 49 (lo), 1403 escapes in total, at most 29 per warp list.
router_design.paths: pw-rtc1 (m 1, 8) and pw-rtc4 (m 16, 32): cluster, grid 8 x 8 (KS 8 is the largest portable cluster), 32 chunks per CTA. pw-rtg16-1 / pw-rtg32-1 (m 1, 8) and pw-rtg16-4 / pw-rtg32-4 (m 16, 32): global, grid 8 x 16 (16 chunks per CTA) and 8 x 32 (8 chunks per CTA). pw-rtg128 (m 128): global, 8 x 32 = 256 CTAs, smem 168 KB (1 CTA/SM, so about 2 waves). smem: 33-168 KB.
router_design.sass: Router hot path per chunk per warp (static count, as for pw7): 71.75 at m<=8 (rc1), 87.1 at m=16/32 (rc4).
router_design.split: hi = bf16(W), lo = bf16(W - hi) (the same split as the template's fallback for m > 8). hi + lo is exact in fp32: hi has 8 significant bits and lo the next 8 (rounded), so their sum needs at most 16 bits. A one-hot row therefore produces exactly 8*hi + 8*lo in any reduction order. That is why the router's one-hot reference is hi.float() + lo.float() and the kernel must reproduce it bit for bit.
router_design.validation: _validate gains an optional exact_w, used only for the router (prepare passes state['router_hl'] = hi.float() + lo.float() when the layer is fp32). One-hot rows must equal it exactly; random rows are checked against FP64 of the original fp32 W within the harness's 2e-5. The judge's bounds are 1e-4 overall and 1e-3 on probe rows; the emulator gives 2-3e-6 against W. The one-hot pass runs at the router's own K = 8192 (x is [m, 8192]), so m=1 is 8192 launches per path for 3 paths (about 3 s), no batching needed.

design.epilogue: Consumer-only named barrier. D (fragment order = the mma.sync C layout) is staged in the drained ring. Then a cluster barrier. Rank r owns a rectangle of the n-block: RTB/KS whole row tiles when KS <= RTB, otherwise one tile x a 1/(KS/RTB) token range. Its threads issue all KS ld.shared::cluster.v4 loads before the adds, write bf16 (fp32 for the router) into a [tokens][rows] smem transpose buffer, then store 16-B row pieces of out. A final cluster barrier keeps peer smem alive. KS = 1 runs without a cluster.
design.kernel: pwg<NWG, NT, ST=4, RTR>. Consumer warpgroups 0..NWG-1 (BN = 64*NWG W rows; warp w of warpgroup i decodes row tile 4i+w = rows 16w..16w+15 of the warpgroup's 64-row block) plus one producer warpgroup (warps 4*NWG..4*NWG+3; one lane issues; with NWG 2 it runs setmaxnreg.dec 40 and the consumers setmaxnreg.inc 232). Stage (1024-aligned, 4 deep) = [x tile NT x 64 k bf16, TMA 2D box {64, NT}, SWIZZLE_128B, rows >= m zero-filled][W chunk RTB x 1536 B, cp.async.bulk], one full barrier with expect_tx = both.
design.m_beyond_256: m > 256 (judge tests 512, 1000) and every odd m are not served by any wgmma path. They run the template fallback (cuBLAS) as before. The kernel itself handles any 1 <= m <= NT through TMA zero fill and masked stores, but only m in {128, 256} are registered.
design.pipeline: Per 64-k chunk u: wait full(u) -> 3 x ld.shared.v4 + pw_dec (+ escape XOR) into A[u & 1] -> fence the accumulators -> wgmma.fence -> 4 x wgmma m64nNk16 (descriptor +32 B per k16 step) -> commit -> wgmma.wait_group 1 (chunk u-1 complete) -> pin A[(u-1) & 1] with asm volatile("" : "+r") -> arrive empty(slot of u-1). The decode of chunk u therefore overlaps the MMAs of chunk u-1. At the end: wait_group 0, release the last slot.
design.removed: pw3's mma.sync TMA x-ring kernel (pwt) and its paths pw-tm / pw-tms (pw-tmh was already gone), plus the helper only it used. No other kernel was removed: the m<=32 and router paths stay byte-identical to pw8, as requested.
design.smem_and_registers: w2n128: 384 threads, 113 KB, 168-register entry cap (consumers use at most R135). w1n128: 256 threads, 89 KB, 138 regs. w2n256: 384 threads, 177 KB, setmaxnreg dealloc 40 / alloc 232 (consumer code up to R199, no spill). w1n256: 256 threads, 153 KB, 203 regs. wr: 256 threads, 153 KB, 203 regs. All 0 spill, 0 local loads/stores.
design.split_k_table: mode a = the largest KS in {1, 2, 4, 8} with NB*KS <= 132; mode b = the next larger one. BN 128 (w2n*): qkv 18x4 = 72 / 18x8 = 144, o 64x2 = 128 / 64x4, pooler 32x4 = 128 / 32x8, unpooler 64x2 = 128 / 64x4. BN 64 (w1n*): qkv 36x2 / 36x4, o 128x1 / 128x2, pooler 64x2 / 64x4, unpooler 128x1 / 128x2. Router (wr, BN 64): 4x8 = 32 CTAs over K' = 16384. KS 7 (from the brief) is not used: rank rectangles must tile the n-block, so KS is limited to divisors of the 8 (or 4) row tiles, or tiles x token ranges.
design.stats: New STATS lines in prepare (before the probes and the BAKE table), one per layer and for router hi / lo: distinct exponents, the smallest exponent window covering 99 / 99.9 / 99.99 / 100% of weights, the escape rate of an 8-code exponent window (centred on the mode, and best), the 16-code (current codec) escape rate, the fraction with 1-3 trailing zero mantissa bits, zeros, subnormals, and the Shannon entropy of the 16-bit value / exponent / mantissa. 1.1 s on CPU for all six. On the reference generator's weights: H16 = 10.46 bits/weight (router lo 10.98), Hexp 2.54, Hman 6.97 (incompressible). An 8-code window leaves 1.25-1.36% escapes (router lo 4.0%); the 16-code window of the 12-bit codec leaves 0.01%.

risks: Nothing here ran on hardware. The emulator checks the layouts, packing and index math against the PTX ISA's documented layouts; a misread of the hardware (descriptor field, swizzle phase, scale-d semantics) shows up as INVALID in the bake (one-hot mismatch), not as a crash. Descriptor addresses stay inside the CTA's stage, so a wrong field cannot address outside shared memory.

Hang risk: the full/empty protocol and both cluster barriers are simulated. The producer warpgroup exits early; the cluster barriers wait only for non-exited threads (PTX), and the epilogue uses a consumer-only named barrier.

x L2 traffic: BN 128 re-reads x once per n-block: 64 MB at m=128 and 128 MB at m=256 for pooler. If the bake shows m=256 below target while m=128 meets it, that is the cause (next: x multicast across a (2, KS) cluster, or BN 256).

Log: STATS (7 lines, about 2.3 KB) prints early, so a long log could push it out of the 16 kB tail. The PW build lines were shortened to '<NG>x<KS>' to keep the total near 12 KB.

Bits are total bits/weight, measured with the prototype on 1M weights, all overheads included. Decode is lane-instructions per weight, from the SASS probes.

- **Overheads.** The bit counts include stream words with tail padding, escapes (32 bits each), one 32-bit stream offset per warp, and 16 units per warp stream. The per-lane layout adds 32 × 16-bit lane starts per segment and costs +0.000–0.009 bits; the prototype prints it for each variable-length design. Per-matrix tables (256 × 4 B LUT, rank map) are excluded; they cost < 0.01 bits on any real matrix.
- **Where variable length helps.** The gain is concentrated in the top-2 h7 values, which cover 85% of weights at about 1 bit of information. A fixed 2-bit code wastes about 0.37 bits there.
- Use pair symbols (rank of w0, rank of w1): 100 symbols, canonical Huffman limited to 8 bits by package-merge.
- That is feasible on issue, but it is no longer hidden for free. Note that the 5.8 includes E's own sign and plane merge, which replaces r6's dec1 entirely.

- **Floor for a per-symbol variable-length decode on this register layout.** Each pair needs at least a length (1–2 ops), a 2-op 64-bit shift, a value lookup (address + LDS) and a 2-op merge into the A register. That is about 7 per pair, plus about 0.5 per weight for refills: **≈ 4 lane-instr/weight**. r6 spends 1.5.

2. **Stage merging.** When the ring has >= 10 stages (K-major NT, one math warpgroup), stages are merged so BLOCK_K becomes 128 or 192 with >= 5 stages; this halves/thirds the number of fence/commit/wait rounds per K (K:45-56). For pooler m=128 the heuristic's 64x64x64, 13 stages becomes **6 stages of 64x64x128 (32 KB/stage, 192 KB in flight), 8 wgmma m64n64k16 per group**.

**Stage merge (K:45-56):** if `kNumStages_ >= 10 && Normal && A,B K-major && math threads == 128`, then `per_merge = kNumStages_ / 5`, `BLOCK_K = 64 * per_merge`, `kNumStages = kNumStages_ / per_merge`. The merged stage is `per_merge` consecutive 64-wide K atoms laid out back to back (A atoms then B atoms per stage); descriptors step `atom_k_idx * BLOCK_M * 64` elements between atoms (K:218, 266-270; MMA:239-241). Allocated smem is still the unmerged 13 (or 15) x stage bytes, so up to one unmerged stage is wasted.
The producer therefore runs up to `kNumStages` stages ahead, including across tile boundaries (it fetches the next tile's first stages while the consumers are in the epilogue).

Empty arrive happens **after `wait_group 0`** of the stage's own group (K:278-281), i.e. a slot is held for TMA latency + full-wait + issue + full MMA drain. There is no early release and no "release stage s-1 after wait_group 1". With 6-16 stages the producer still has >= 5 stages of lookahead per Little's-law budget. This is the part our pw10 ladder identified as the exposed-wgmma cost at 4 stages; DeepGEMM compensates only with depth (192-216 KB in flight) and the merged BLOCK_K.
